The harsh reality of non-fiction writing

Sorry, but my overall reaction to that article is: diddums. This is an industry where even the professionals acknowledge you might sell at maximum 5,000 copies, which is pretty much not possible. It is built entirely on self-delusion.

If you want to write history, write fucking history and market to historians or people who like histories. If you want to write a book setting out your own life experiences as if you did something truly unique or came to some earth-shattering insight that completely changes the human condition, be content with an audience of one or rename yourself Jesus Christ.

Let's review the five finalists for the non-fiction literary prize:

With the exception of historian David O’Keefe’s One Day In August: The Untold Story Behind Canada’s Tragedy at Dieppe, for the first time in the award’s history, four out of five finalists are works of memoir. Plum Johnson’s They Left Us Everything is an exploration of grief and the meaning of material possessions; M.G. Vassanji’s And Home Was Kariakoo: A Memoir of East Africa, finds the two-time Giller Prize-winner returning to, and attempting to understand, the place where he was born and raised; Barbara Taylor’s The Last Asylum: A Memoir of Madness in Our Times is both a cultural history of mental health care and a raw portrait of troubled life; and Kathleen Winter’s Boundless: Tracing Land and Dream in a New Northwest Passage, which chronicles the author’s two-week voyage to the Far North, is both a family memoir and a lucid travelogue of a place most of us will never visit.

I would lay you five bucks that of these, only the first book will sell more than two hundred copies in the real world. They say don't judge a book by its cover, but let's be really, really honest: does anyone really feel inspired or inclined to dash out and buy any of those books going by their subject matter? All four of these memoirs strike me as bound narcissism, most likely riddled with leftie shit. It doesn't matter how many out-of-touch academic groups say a book is "important": if people don't read it, it's not. That Boundless book in particular is treading ground that's been done before and done better: try Gavin Francis's True North or The Final Frontiersman.

Want to know the easiest way to sell more copies of these memoirs and bring some attention to your subject area of interest? Cloak it in a fantasy world or a science-fiction equivalent and then publicise the fact you basically templated it off your life/your area of interest.
